name: General table
summary: The fallback for any table no other type fits: it learns what one row is, which numbers matter, what the codes mean and where the data comes from. It never wins on header score and runs only when nothing else is a candidate or the owner says none fit.

goals.label: Understand what's in it
goals.desc: I'd write a plain guide to every column

goals.label: Answer a question with it
goals.desc: I'd pull the numbers that answer it

goals.label: Connect it to another sheet
goals.desc: I'd find the columns that match

goals.label: Automate it
goals.desc: I'd sketch an app that does this work

questions.prompt: What is one row in this table?
questions.why: Every count and total depends on what one row stands for.

fact.statement: One row in this table is, per the owner: {answer_labels}. {answer_text}

questions.prompt: {rows:amount} rows have a number in {role:amount}. Which kinds of numbers matter most here? Pick all that apply.
questions.why: The numbers you care about are the ones worth checking, totaling and explaining.

fact.statement: The numbers that matter most here, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: {role:amount} has {rows:amount} numbers, such as {values:amount}. What unit are they in?
questions.why: A total is only meaningful when everyone reads it in the same unit.

fact.statement: {role:amount} is stated in, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: Are there rows I should always leave out? Pick all that apply.
questions.recommend_basis: Total rows restate the rows above them, so counting them doubles the numbers.
questions.why: One stray total row can double every sum in the sheet.

fact.statement: The owner said to leave these out of counts and totals: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: {role:category} uses {count:category} short codes such as {values:category}. What do they stand for?

options.label: Another tab explains them
options.desc: A tab or file; name it

questions.why: Codes only the author can read are the knowledge that leaves when the author does.

questions.prompt: Where does this data come from?
questions.why: An export can be refreshed from its system; hand-typed data needs its owner.

fact.statement: This data comes from, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: How often does this data change?
questions.why: It sets how long each note stays current before it is worth a second look.

fact.statement: This data changes this often, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: {role:record_key} has {count:record_key} different values. Which column should connect this sheet to your other file?
questions.why: The right matching column decides how many rows line up across files.

fact.statement: This sheet connects to other files on, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: When new rows arrive, what should happen?
questions.why: An app is only worth sketching around the job the new rows trigger.

fact.statement: When new rows arrive, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

outputs.title: Data dictionary
outputs.pitch: Data dictionary: every column with what it means, its type, how full it is and example values, checked with you.

outputs.title: Data health check
outputs.pitch: Data health check: blanks, duplicates, odd values and total rows, column by column.

outputs.title: Breakdown
outputs.pitch: Breakdown: {role:amount} by {role:category} and over time, largest first, with total rows left out.

outputs.title: Connected view
outputs.pitch: Connected view: this sheet matched to your other file, with how many rows line up on each side.

outputs.title: Guide for the next owner
outputs.pitch: Guide for the next owner: a plain page on what this sheet is, what one row is, what each column and code means, where the data comes from and how often it changes.

outputs.title: App blueprint
outputs.pitch: App blueprint: a small app built around this sheet's job, with the columns as a form, the rules as checks and the new-row step automated.

gotchas.say: {role:record_key} may have lost leading zeros or long digits in Excel, so a code like 00123 can show as 123.
{role:amount} is blank on some rows; blanks and zeros mean different things and are counted separately.
One tab is mostly formulas over another, so its numbers restate the source tab rather than add to it.
{role:percent} holds rates, which cannot be added up; a plain average of rates weighs every row the same.
This table has more than one date column, and trends change depending on which one is used.
{role:notes} can hold remarks about people. Those stay on this machine and never go into the file.
{role:category} holds short codes such as {values:category}, whose meaning lives in someone's head unless it is written down.

graph.sentence: Dots are the tabs and columns of this file. Lines show which columns connect or depend on each other. Bigger means more rows.
